title: How Fast You Walk May Determine How Long You Live - Nautilus
content:
You don’t actually need to take 10,000 steps a day to stay fit. That figure comes from the marketing campaign for a Japanese pedometer called the Manpo-Kei, which translates to “10,000 steps meter.” It’s proved to be a remarkably resilient myth, though. 

Featured Video

So how many steps should you take per day? A new study published in the British Journal of Sports Medicine has some answers.

Physical activity researchers from the University of Sydney tracked the steps and walking pace of more than 100,000 middle-aged adults enrolled in the U.K.’s BioBank program for seven consecutive days. They then followed their health for roughly eight years to record any differences in mortality between four separate groups: those who took less than 5,000 steps per day; those who took between 5,000 and 7,500; those who took between 7,500 and 10,000; and the overachievers who averaged more than 10,000 steps. During the study period, nearly 1,700 of the participants passed away, and around 500 of them died of cardiovascular disease. 

Read more: “Here’s Why Our Walking Gets Slower As We Age”

Interestingly, the researchers found several different combinations of steps and pace associated with a reduced risk for premature death. People taking less than 5,000 steps per day saw a substantially reduced risk of mortality, but only if their pace was brisk (80 steps per minute). In fact, people taking these short, quick walks had the same risk of premature death as those who walked between 5,000 and 7,500 steps per day at a slow pace (60 steps per minute).

According to the researchers, the key seems to be walking at a speedy clip for at least half an hour per day. Those who did so showed a progressively reduced risk of death from any cause—at least among the groups walking less than 7,500 steps per day.

But what about the others? 

People walking between 7,500 and 10,000 steps seemed to be the healthiest, with their premature mortality risk reduced the most, even compared to those taking more than 10,000 steps. Per the team, the human body runs into diminishing returns around that mark. 

So, again, there’s no need to take 10,000 steps a day, but you may want to pick up the pace a little when you are out and about.

title: The 17 Minutes That Changed America
author: Krista Stevens
content:
If you make time for one 9/11 anniversary story this year, make it Garrett M. Graff’s piece. This is no mere retrospective. For National Geographic, Graff takes us through that Tuesday morning 25 years ago to explain how America lost its sense of security, minute-by-minute on the morning of September 11, 2001.

It was now 8:53 a.m. There were just 10 minutes left in America as we knew it.

FBI director Robert Mueller was in his first week on the job, sitting in his office suite on the seventh floor of the J. Edgar Hoover Building in Washington. . . .Toward the end of the meeting, someone interrupted to tell Mueller a plane had crashed in New York. Sitting in a briefing on al Qaeda, deep in a conversation about terrorism, Mueller turned and looked out the window at the blue sky beyond and asked, “How could a plane not see the tower? It’s so clear out today.”

Truthfully, terrorism in 2001 just wasn’t something most Americans thought about, outside of the movies or the occasional evening news story or headline. It was a plot device for thrillers, not a perpetual source of anxiety at shopping malls, schools, or public events. And even in the cinema, the “terrorists” were less ideological enemies doing existential battle against the Great Satan and more often the disgruntled genius or vaguely European criminal mastermind. Think Dennis Hopper’s villainous former bomb squad officer in the 1994 blockbuster Speed or Alan Rickman’s turn as the suave, ruthless radical Hans Gruber in Die Hard.

More stories about 9/11

Jennifer Senior | The Atlantic | August 9, 2021 | 13,254 words

Garrett M. Graff | Politico | September 11, 2020 | 9,596 words

title: Gloria Steinem Gave It All
author: @NewYorker
content:
It is Wednesday, August 12th, almost four weeks after my last visit with Gloria Steinem in New York. I am in Formentera, a small, windswept island off the eastern coast of Spain, revered for its lack of machinery, to watch the solar eclipse. At half past eight in the evening, there is still daylight, in what will turn out to be the hottest August recorded here since 1961. A crowd is starting to form at the beach. Sweat is running down the backs of my legs, and beside me, a small child is digging a hole in the sand—something pointless and therefore extremely important, in the way things done by children often are.

A cloud has stationed itself precisely where the eclipse is meant to be, but the light changes anyway, not quite into night but into something stranger, as though somebody has reached for the dimmer switch on the world, turned it down, and then slowly turned it back up again. A hush passes from person to person until hundreds of us are standing together, looking upward.

The day before, I received a message from Amy, Gloria’s longtime friend, explaining that Gloria had been mostly in bed since I last saw her. I go back and listen to the first interview that Gloria and I did together, at the Emmanuel Centre, in London, almost ten years ago, not long after we first met. We spoke about her memoir “My Life on the Road,” erotica, the political scientist Valerie Hudson, and the problem of gender inequality—its unnerving invisibility, and its enormous scale. Maddeningly, almost everything we talked about is even more relevant today than it was then.

Listening to the interview through my car speaker, I can hear myself trying to figure out, in real time, how the hell she does it: how she is so at ease with herself, so grounded in her opinions without ever becoming rigid, how someone can possess convictions that strong and yet wear them that lightly. Most of all, I am in awe of her authenticity; there appeared to be almost no gap between the woman and what she believed.

The last time I saw her, on July 15th, I had gone to her brownstone, which has served as an organizing and gathering space for activists, writers, and political figures for more than fifty years. The whole place says “history.” The walls are the color of mustard; fabrics and tapestries are everywhere—it is a space that has accumulated rather than acquired its beauty. In the living room, a pair of sirens sits on the wooden mantelpiece. Around the fireplace is a deep-green club fender. Picture frames, plants, and talismans cover all available wall and table space. (For someone who has lived a life of such import, fragments of memory seem surprisingly precious to her.) A small kitchen sits off to one side, and the low ceiling makes the ground floor feel less like a formal living room and more like a club or meeting space. The domestic and the political don’t seem, here, to have been assigned separate rooms.

I remember noticing Gloria’s hands the first time we met, the way her fingernails were carefully shaped and slightly long, a detail of herself she consistently attended to. There was a femininity and a fragility to them that I hadn’t picked up on in photographs. They were always like this when I saw her. Her hair was always in its bob. She was always in black, with a concha belt slung around her waist. That day, she sat in the middle of her low sofa, surrounded by papers and undrunk cups of liquid, looking thinner than she did when I last saw her.

Gloria and I had always talked about marriage and its symbolism—what the institution has meant for women, what we inherit from it, what might be reclaimed or reinvented. Halfway through our conversation, I showed Gloria my own hands, and the ring on my left ring finger, which is meant to represent a different kind of union: a marriage to life itself. I found myself crouched on the floor in front of her, my bare knees on the carpet, explaining the concept, and I felt, very strongly, the sense of something having been passed and shared between us, and I was proud—proud to show her something I had made from ideas we had spent years turning over together.

Eventually, Gloria had to go upstairs for another appointment. Before she disappeared up the spiral staircase, I asked if I could hug her goodbye. As I pressed my body to hers, trying to wrap my arms around her carefully, I knew, with a peculiar certainty, that this would be the last time I saw her.

I have always felt a strange protectiveness toward Gloria, which is absurd when you consider that Gloria Steinem has spent her life protecting the rest of us. She is one of the greatest heroines of the twentieth century.

After the 2016 election, I cried, because I realized that Gloria might die without seeing a woman become President of the United States. There was something unbearable about watching her give almost the whole span of her adult life to democracy, to women, to the stubborn proposition that human beings might organize themselves more fairly, and still never see that particular threshold crossed. I also feared the coming assault on the rights that Gloria had worked so hard to protect.

I remember a male friend telling me that I was overreacting, and that it wasn’t going to be that big of a deal. I stared at the television and said, “They’ll go after Roe v. Wade.” The threat had been stated plainly for years; perhaps what was required was simply the willingness to believe people when they told you what they intended to do.

Gloria somehow held the urgency of it all without ever losing her lightness. When I first began getting to know her, I was anxious: Was I feminist enough, had I read enough, would I pass some imagined female purity test? Gloria gently dismantled the premise. People, she explained, are where they are in their journey of discovery and learning, and feminism had to meet them there. I didn’t have to arrive already knowing everything in order to belong.

Gloria was radical in the original sense of the word, which is derived from the Latin radix, meaning “root”—going to the system underneath the problem rather than attempting to remedy its surface effects—and she somehow held that radicalism alongside an almost unreasonable kindness. I have tried to carry that forward—to hold myself to account while understanding that patriarchy is not something women stand conveniently outside of. We were born inside it; it lives inside us. It has shaped our ideas of beauty, love, goodness, success, and safety, and we cannot simply announce ourselves liberated and be done with it. We can only begin to rectify something after we recognize it; we can only shed a skin once we have outgrown it.

Before leaving Gloria’s brownstone, I had given her a card I had bought in New York, made by the artist Olga Prinku, depicting a glittery silver snake. On the day of the eclipse, I look up what the snake means: transformation, rebirth, healing, knowledge—and feminine power. What a complicated creature we chose for this symbol. I think of the lion, that familiar emblem of masculine power, with his soft, beige fur and magnificent mane, made harmless enough in miniature that little boys sleep with him tucked under their arms. Women get the snake: close to the ground, frightening, blamed for the fall of man, and periodically required to split its own skin open in order to grow.

Gloria seemed to know the same thing about people, that change involves a certain kind of splitting. She could be radical without requiring everyone to arrive at the same revelation at the same moment, and held that generosity alongside an increasingly radical article of faith—her belief in democracy, even as so many of its believers began to wonder whether the whole experiment had failed.

Her papers at Smith College now occupy a hundred and six feet of shelf space. There are very few people I have met about whom I can say, with certainty, that they gave the whole thing, not merely the public bit but the private Tuesdays, too—the days when nobody was watching, when the work was fashionable and when it wasn’t, when there was hope and when hope itself must have required considerable imagination.

When I try to think of the small, funny details that could cut the sadness of writing this—the sorts of things these pieces need—I come up strangely empty-handed. I never ate a burrito with Gloria. We worked together. We talked politics. We talked about books; she gave me books, so many that I sheepishly had to ask her for a tote bag, too, in order to carry them all.

As the eclipse passes, I think about how quiet I have been for quite some time now, and I realize that something about that has to change, because if Gloria is leaving us, then some of us are going to have to get louder. It feels less like a decision than like a law of physics: I think of gravity, of black holes, of the way one body continues to exert a force on another across apparently empty space. I feel Gloria’s gravity still, pulling me toward the horizon and toward a world she could already envision.

She did not get to see it.

Perhaps I won’t either. But this may be the difficult truth about progress that Gloria understood better than most of us: you may spend your whole life walking toward a world you will never enter, but that does not relieve you of the obligation to walk.

The snake does not repair its old skin. The snake outgrows it, pressing itself against the earth, against rock, against whatever will give it enough resistance to begin the challenging work of leaving one form behind. In Formentera, I watch the moon move through shadow and back toward the light, and, for a moment, it seems as if the whole world is changing its skin. ♦

title: Court Grants TRO Barring "Threatening, Intimidating, and Retaliation Action ... Without a Legitimate Law Enforcement Purpose" Against ICE Watcher
content:
From Judge Michael Newman (S.D. Ohio) Friday in Moorman v. Doe No. 1; since this is a decision at the temporary restraining order stage, the factual assertions are preliminary conclusions by the judge, not final findings of fact:

Plaintiff Sean Moorman … alleges Defendants—seven unidentified United States Immigration and Customs Enforcement ("ICE") officers, in their official capacities—have retaliated (and continue to retaliate) against him for engaging in activity protected by the First Amendment ….

The motion for TRO was filed around 7 P.M. on Tuesday, September 1, 2026. The Court heard extensive oral argument the next day at 4 P.M., lasting more than one hour…. At the time of the phone conference, the AUSA [who represented the government -EV] failed to contradict the Moorman's factual assertions and requested a two-week extension to file a response brief. As detailed herein, based on the serious nature of the allegations involved, and the threat of ongoing constitutional violations, this extension would be inappropriate. See Elrod v. Burns (1976) ("The loss of First Amendment freedoms, for even minimal periods of time, unquestionably constitutes irreparable injury.")….

Moorman volunteers as an "ICE watcher" in his spare time. As uncontradicted by the AUSA, Moorman "lawfully and peacefully" documents interactions between ICE officers and the Springfield community, noting potentially violent or unlawful action by ICE officers….

According to Moorman, by August 20, 2026, certain ICE officers had identified Moorman as an ICE watcher and began "lashing out" at him.  Specifically, on August 20, 2026, Moorman recorded … [an] ICE vehicle driven by Defendant John Doe No. 2…. "John Doe No. 2 turned his Jeep around and accelerated dangerously towards [Moorman]'s vehicle as though to ram it, before veering away at the last moment and disappearing."

The next morning, on August 21, 2026, Moorman stood on the side of a main road in Springfield alongside a reporter wearing a press badge, and recorded ICE officers conducting an arrest. An ICE officer wearing a yellow vest, identified as Defendant John Doe No. 1, approached Moorman and the reporter, put his phone in their faces as if to scan or take a picture, and then continued walking.

Later that day, Moorman entered the parking lot of a Cracker Barrel restaurant in Springfield to observe and photograph ICE officers after identifying [other] known ICE vehicles…. Upon seeing Moorman enter the parking lot, the ICE officers, who had just exited their vehicles, immediately re-entered their vehicles. Moorman observed Defendant John Doe No. 1 looking at him with binoculars.

The ICE officers then pulled out of their parking spots. As Moorman proceeded to exit the parking lot, the ICE officers "looped around and followed [him]." With the ICE officers following him, Moorman circled around the Cracker Barrel, another adjacent parking lot, and an adjacent dead-end road.

After a few minutes, Moorman and the ICE officers returned to the Cracker Barrel parking lot. Each time Moorman pulled into a parking spot, the ICE officers would pull in front of and block Moorman's vehicle and prevent him from moving out of his spot. The ICE officers would each block Moorman's vehicle for ten seconds at a time, sometimes taking photos of his license plate, before allowing him to move to another location in the parking lot. This happened for the next ten to fifteen minutes. Throughout this encounter, Moorman put his vehicle into park each time the ICE officers were in front of him and kept his hands on the steering wheel so that the officers could see them.

Moorman eventually was able to exit the Cracker Barrel parking lot but ended up on a dead-end road nearby. At that point, Moorman was approached by the Nissan Pathfinder driven by Defendant John Doe No. 3, who was masked and wearing large sunglasses. The officer waved at Moorman, apparently signaling Moorman to follow him; Moorman complied with the officer's direction.

As Moorman followed the Nissan Pathfinder, a Hyundai Sante Fe driven by Defendant John Doe No. 1, followed behind Moorman. The ICE officers led Moorman toward a rural area on the outskirts of Springfield where Moorman and his wife live. During oral argument, the AUSA offered no explanation for the ICE officers' leading Moorman back to his residence.

Upon realizing this, Moorman called other volunteer ICE watchers to warn them about the situation. He also called his wife, who was home alone with their pets, and told her that ICE officers were heading toward their home, and to lock the doors and stay inside. Moorman's wife cowered in the house holding a baseball bat out of fear.

The Nissan Pathfinder then pulled up to the end of Moorman's driveway and slowed. Defendant John Doe No. 3 put his arm out of the vehicle's window and pointed at Moorman's house. He took pictures of Moorman and his wife's vehicles. After this encounter, Moorman and his wife installed a security camera at their home and now keep their doors locked at all times.

ICE officers continued to engage with Moorman throughout the next several days. [Further details omitted for space reasons. -EV] …

The Court takes notice that national incidents similar to those described herein have devolved into circumstances leading to serious injury or loss of life to officers and members of the community alike….

Moorman seeks a TRO enjoining Defendants, and those acting in concert with them, from "taking further threatening, intimidating, and retaliatory action against [him] in response to his exercise of his First Amendment rights … without a legitimate law enforcement purpose." According to Moorman, such actions include, but are not limited to, pursuing his vehicle, attempting to box in his vehicle, approaching him, traveling to his home, or shouting at him to intimidate him, without a legitimate law enforcement purpose. While these events considered seriatim would be less concerning, when considering the allegations together, they amount to a substantial and troubling violation of Moorman's First Amendment rights….

First, Moorman engaged, and continues to engage, in protected conduct. Eight circuits have expressly held that filming government agents performing official duties in public is protected under the First Amendment. Other courts in this district have also recognized this right….

While some courts have imposed reasonable time, place, and manner restrictions on an individual's right to record law enforcement, the record shows that Moorman conducts his ICE watching activities in a safe and lawful manner; he records ICE activity only while in public spaces, takes precautions to make sure he is not threatening officers' safety such as keeping his hands visible, follows applicable traffic laws, and does not interfere with ICE's enforcement operations. Moorman has also participated in specific training for individuals who wish to monitor law enforcement activity in a safe, lawful, and peaceful manner.

Second, Moorman has suffered adverse action(s). An adverse action is one that "would deter a person of ordinary firmness from continuing to engage in" protected conduct under the First Amendment….

While some retaliatory acts are so de minimis that "they do not rise to the level of being constitutional violations," Defendants' actions in this case surpass that threshold…. Moorman asserts that Defendants, over the course of several days, nearly swerved into his vehicle; scouted Moorman's home for no legitimate purpose (on multiple occasions) causing Moorman's wife to fear for her safety; continuously stalked Moorman around Springfield; and cut off and trapped Moorman's vehicle in a parking lot. At minimum, ICE officers seized Moorman in the Cracker Barrel parking lot on August 21, 2026, see U.S. v. See (6th Cir. 2009) (noting that blocking a person's car with a patrol car was a warrantless seizure), thus constituting adverse action. See Wood v. Eubanks (6th Cir. 2022) (holding that a Fourth Amendment seizure amounts to an adverse action for the purpose of a First Amendment retaliation claim).

Finally, Moorman has demonstrated a causal connection between his protected conduct and the adverse actions allegedly perpetrated by Defendants…. Defendants remain free at a later stage to show that they would have taken the same action regardless of Moorman's protected conduct. However, at this time, nothing in the record supports that showing, and Moorman need only demonstrate a likelihood of success, not a certainty.

Here, Defendants cannot identify a single, legitimate basis for continuing to harass and intimidate Moorman for exercising his First Amendment rights. Defendants, and others acting in concert with them, including all other ICE officers stationed in Springfield, Ohio, will suffer no cognizable harm from a TRO that does no more than require them to comply with the Constitution they are already bound, and have sworn, to follow. Moreover, it is always in the public interest to enjoin unconstitutional conduct.

Moorman's proposed TRO is limited in scope; it requests that Defendants refrain from harassing and committing retaliatory acts—including pursuing his vehicle, approaching him, photographing him in a threatening manner, traveling to his home, or shouting at him for the purposes of intimidation—without a legitimate law enforcement purpose.

To that end, two items merit mention. First, the Court is not telling ICE— part of the executive branch—how to do its job.

Second, the Court is not entering into the political fray to suggest whether or not ICE should be engaging in deportation activities in Springfield, Ohio.

What the Court is holding is that, when government actors engage in such conduct, the Constitution requires that it be undertaken without hazing, retaliation, or harassment, particularly with regard to an individual who does not interfere with ICE's enforcement function or police power. As Justice [Gorsuch] aptly said, the "Government is not free to disregard the First Amendment in times of crisis." Roman Catholic v. Diocese of Brooklyn v. Cuomo (2020) (Gorsuch, J.) (concurring) ….

David J. Carey, Freda J. Levenson, and Carlen Zhang-D'Souza (ACLU of Ohio) represent plaintiff.

title: Grandmaster Flash’s Remix of Hip-Hop History
author: @NewYorker
content:
Check out a dance floor the next time you get a chance. Take note at the point in a song when the real dancers stop messing around. (“That was my part,” one of them might later say, or, like the grownups I used to know, “It got good to me.”) Usually, it has something to do with drums. A snare, or a kick, or a tom, or the rattle of an 808 tickles something in the groin or the hips, and the focus of the dancers sharpens. Their movements become more spiteful than woo-woo, more sculpture than painting, more an argument than an idle thought. Now, the sorcery of the dance floor is that this is never happening to only one dancer. This thing with the beat, the heightened part of the song that makes the room get suddenly serious—somehow it’s as objective as math, observable by everybody in the room. The drum hits just so, and it gets good to a whole crowd, all at once. Somebody cries out “Ay!!!” or “Whooo!!!” to acknowledge what’s going on.

One of the luckiest art-related miracles of the past century or so is that there was a young boy named Joseph Saddler, who’d later go by the name Grandmaster Flash and become the Promethean d.j. whose technique on the turntables would help usher into being the mix of sounds and attitudes that we now call hip-hop. Joseph got so obsessed with this moment of collective frenzy, and frustrated by the fleetingness of the part of the song that made it happen, that he spent his life learning to extend it indefinitely. In his new book, “Birth of a Culture” (Amistad), written with Scoop Jackson, Flash reminisces about spying on parties put on by his parents and older sisters. A favorite song at these parties was Curtis Mayfield’s “Move On Up”:

It’s 1970 and this is when I started paying scientific attention to the drum beat. That song had the world’s longest drum break—it had to be two minutes or more. I would get lost in that drum break, trapped. So when I started listening to other records, I’d notice that when the drum break came in, the backsides of my mom and dad’s friends would move more. Their behinds gyrated with more purpose; their dancing seemed to become more intense and serious. So, in my toddler mind, the best part of the record has to be when the least of the band members were playing in accompaniment with the drummer. They called it “the drum solo”—whether it be the drummer and the bass player, the drummer and the cellist, or the drummer and the trumpet, to any other instrument in connection with the drummer. This was very exciting for me. My thought was that all records had this long drum solo like Curtis Mayfield’s record. As I was listening to other artists, to my disappointment, the drum solo on other records was over as soon as I blinked my eyes.

It’s funny: the great Grandmaster Flash, born in 1958, in the Bronx, calls himself a “toddler” in this anecdote, even though he was twelve at the time. Maybe this is because he views his adolescent self, enjoying a sensual perception whose implications he hadn’t yet begun to puzzle through, as still a baby in the context of the history of the music he’d eventually help invent. From the beginning, he had a scientific cast of mind, and not only about the fervors of dance. Confronted with the mystery of his father’s nighttime habit of listening to records—where’s the music coming from, and what does it have to do with this needle and that black disk?—Flash sneaked, over and over, despite many hard-handed spankings from his dad, into the closet that housed the vinyl.

Joseph, Sr., was physically abusive to his wife, as well as his son, and before long the family split up. Flash and his siblings moved with their mom from Throggs Neck to Fox Street, in the South Bronx. Amid so much chaos, and perhaps—although Flash never makes this connection—because of it, Joseph, Jr., hyper-fixated on electronics. He ripped apart record players and other gadgets, terrorizing the rest of his family with his curiosity and his surgeon’s willingness to attempt to operate on the bodies of household appliances. The tunnel vision that would make him a genius to the wider world first marked him as bad at home.

His mother had the wisdom to send him to a vocational-and-technical school where Flash learned the rudiments of amplified sound. Soon, he could put the gadgets back together, and even produce versions of them. Pining after the power of the disco d.j.s on the radio, he made his own d.j. set. But he still wanted to know: How could he keep the best parts of his favorite songs playing over and over? “The root of everything I was trying to discover was based on science and math,” he wrote.

Flash tricked out his homemade d.j. set, adding a felt bed for his records instead of the standard metal platter. He marked up the surface of his vinyls with crayons so that he could know when exactly the “break” of a song—the drum break that dependably made the partyers go wild—began and ended. He then figured out a blasphemous move: touching the surface of the records with his fingers to drag them in the opposite direction of the turntable’s motion, thus starting the break over. He used two copies of every record—toggling back and forth, catching the beat each go-round with impeccable timing, giving the illusion that the drum break never stopped, that it had always, at least implicitly, been a slice of something infinite, and that now, under his trance, it would never stop, until he gave it a chance to mercifully die. Then he mixed one break with another, sometimes letting them bleed together, sometimes making an abrupt switch that felt like a natural fact. True to his lifelong experimental bent, he called his invention the Quik Mix Theory.

Flash knew of the two other d.j.s who were working in the Bronx at the time, with whom he’d later share credit for the genesis of hip-hop. There was Kool Herc, who was one of the pioneers of the “needle drop” technique for extending breaks, and who had the best speaker setup in town. And there was Afrika Bambaataa, who had the widest and most cosmopolitan collection of records of the three, the most sophisticated sense of the history of Black sound, and a reputation for uniting rival gangs and reorienting them toward peaceful community aims. Neither, though, had the technical mastery of Flash, nor did they have his knack for the mathematics of the dance floor. Flash would glide from break to break, taking parts of the Incredible Bongo Band’s rendition of “Apache”—whose great effect, according to his “science,” “was the way they put the reverb on the snare,” their kick like “thunder and lightning”—and fitting them together with, say, “Heaven and Hell Is on Earth,” by 20th Century Steel Band, knitting a quilt of sometimes quite disparate older music and making of it something thrillingly new. He couldn’t stand to let the tension drop for even a second. If hip-hop seems excessive, this is why: its sound was invented, at least in part, to deliver too much of a good thing.

The early chapters of “Birth of a Culture” are devoted to telling Grandmaster Flash’s origin story, but the rest of the book is an episodic telling of hip-hop’s later history; Flash talks about or interviews rappers such as LL Cool J and Q-Tip in order to establish bonds of continuity between his achievement and theirs. (His first book, “The Adventures of Grandmaster Flash: My Life, My Beats,” from 2008, was a more straightforward memoir.) He is careful not to make his accomplishments, or hip-hop itself, sound like the product of a solitary genius. He always gives credit to Herc and Bambaataa, despite his personal (and, often, sonic) conflicts with the former. And he points out the aspects of life in the tough South Bronx—“no crystal stair,” to borrow a phrase from Langston Hughes—which enabled the rise of hip-hop. A party at 1520 Sedgwick Avenue, on August 11, 1973, thrown by Herc and his sister, has been mythologized as the unofficial beginning of the genre, but the truth is that throughout the seventies there were dozens of events like this, many of them held outdoors, in parks. Flash would rewire a street light to provide power for his turntables and speakers, and local kids—usually girls—passed out fliers and served as impromptu publicity teams. Shared space and equipment were put to rogue purposes, funkily repurposing municipal goods for the people. The d.j.s practiced in community centers and Police Athletic League locations, or, say, in the basement of a building where somebody’s dad was the superintendent or had otherwise come into possession of a spare key. Parents of friends would give Flash records from their collections, scarcely aware of what transformations their dusty music would undergo. A neighborhood girl named Anna, according to Flash, improvised the word “hip-hop” while drilling her brother who had signed up for the military:

Cookie started teasing their brother in cadence, “Your left, your left, your left, right, left!” And as she was doing that the other girls, including Anna, were saying, “Hip-hop-hip-hop, it don’t stop,” in the same military-type cadence, but with a rhythm like we were at a jam. She said they were doing that because that’s the way the soldiers walked. “One-two-one-two, pivot, turn, one-two-one-two.”

Anna, in Flash’s telling, was a kind of verbal virtuoso, a proto-rapper who rallied her similarly talented girlfriends to provide lines for the largely male m.c.s who rhymed over Flash’s soundscapes. The point of these anecdotes isn’t to direct sole credit to Anna—there are many rival accounts of the origin of the name “hip-hop”—but to illustrate the communal nature of the beginnings of the music and the culture.

This teeming togetherness becomes evident even in Flash’s music. Listen, for instance, to “The Adventures of Grandmaster Flash on the Wheels of Steel,” from 1981, the first record to showcase the Quik Mix Theory. During the recording session, Flash used three turntables instead of the customary two, so urgently did he feel the need to crowd the song with intriguing earfuls. The cut luxuriates in the pure sound of the songs that make up its collage. The cool, feline bass lines from Queen’s “Another One Bites the Dust” and Blondie’s “Rapture” are enlisted to form a spine, jangling against each other with a dissonant elegance. A snippet of the falsetto vocal from “Good Times,” by Chic, materializes and dissolves like a sun shower. “Apache,” that favorite track of the nascent hip-hop cognoscenti, appears with a knowing wink. Each of these references is made to dance via hypnotic repetition, each graffitied by the sleek scratches that Flash made with his fingers on the vinyl.

Flash is always, in different ways, calling himself a cloistered geek in his book. But “The Adventures of Grandmaster Flash” is the work of a confident cosmopolitan, someone who achieves his most important education outside on the streets, after dark. The scenario that comes to mind is of standing on a city corner at the promising beginning of a hot Saturday night, under a blue-black sky, perhaps waiting for a group of friends to show up, listening with a passive intensity to the music pouring out of car windows as they speed by. The rock kids, the funk kids, the disco-ers, the club rats are all fleetingly conjoined by one pair of highly attuned ears loitering on the streets. It’s the ultimate dance music, the flowering of Flash’s initial desire: to keep the liveliest part of the party going forever.

New York City in the seventies and early eighties, the crucial backdrop for hip-hop’s rise, was a Technicolor place of exaggerated ironies. In 1975, banks stopped underwriting the city’s daunting debt, which caused a fiscal crisis. The answer was austerity. Layoffs swept New York, and youth services suffered cutbacks. People left in droves. Landlords in search of insurance payouts set fire—often fatally—to abandoned buildings in the Bronx, dozens at a time at the height of the phenomenon; the now famous conflagrations glowed like bright symbols of urban decay. Drugs ravaged the streets, leaving needles and even more emptiness in their wake.

But the hollowed-out city became an impromptu stage, especially for the Black teen-agers who, in ad-hoc and decentralized fits and starts, bred the culture with which Flash is so clearly still besotted. Privation couldn’t stop the creative urge. Kids were spray-painting impressive murals on the sides of buildings and the bodies of subway cars. Others practiced a new form of highly kinetic, implicitly aggressive dance which would later be called b-boying, or break dancing. One of these early hip-hoppers was Flash’s eventual friend Fred Brathwaite, known on the streets as Fab 5 Freddy. Earlier this year, Freddy released his own memoir, “Everybody’s Fly.” He was a natural sophisticate whose father was close friends with the jazz drummer Max Roach, and he was a lifelong museumgoer who didn’t understand why he and his fellow-graffitiers couldn’t be considered fine artists. He came into the company of Jean-Michel Basquiat and Keith Haring, plus Debbie Harry from Blondie.

Hip-hop wasn’t the only growing vogue—punk was coming of age, and New Wave was becoming more popular. Black or white, uptown or downtown, it was art-obsessed kids who gave New York its brilliant spark back. Freddy straddled all these worlds, observing their points of intersection and grooves of adjacency. In his book, he muses, for instance, about how “dancehall reggae’s toasting, New York City’s mobile d.j. scene, and rap developed almost simultaneously . . . largely inspired by slick, jive-talking Black disc jockeys on the radio.” And he was dazzled by Flash, too, whose heretically physical way with records—touching and scratching the vinyl like a vandal—reminded him of the heedless white kids he’d come to know downtown. “He was breaking all the rules, which was the most punk thing you could do,” Freddy writes of Flash. “Rap and punk: They were both so wrong they were right.”

Lots of people were running around the Bronx with the name Grandmaster back in the day—a d.j. named Grandmaster Flowers was first, according to Flash. Grandmaster Caz, of the Cold Crush Brothers, was another. Nothing too new there. As a kid, I always wondered if that title, this in-group’s slightly humorous mark of high-ranking nobility, was a fly retort to the dorky Grand Wizards of the Ku Klux Klan, the dangerous losers in the pointy hats with so much terror on their minds. The realm of racism and hatred and death, that kingdom whose violence had spurred the Great Migration, which had in turn created the sometimes harrowing urban conditions that gave hip-hop its environment and raison d’être—they had their weird nomenclature, so why not us?

“Birth of a Culture” might have a similar joke embedded in its title, sharing, as it does, a phrasal structure with “The Birth of a Nation,” D. W. Griffith’s racist apologia for the K.K.K., which also happened to be the first-ever multi-reel blockbuster. Like all of hip-hop’s early heroes, Flash is fixated on the genre’s history—righting its wrongs, fighting a headwind of faulty tellings over the years. He knows that the practice of d.j.’ing—the real origin of hip-hop—has long since been overshadowed by the art of rapping. (He helped this along, too, by recruiting talented rappers—guys nicknamed Kidd Creole, Melle Mel, Scorpio, Cowboy, and Rahiem—to form his backing group, the Furious Five.) But, still, he feels he has to get things straight, perhaps because he knows that the power of a people, and of a culture, comes in part from the practice of fruitfully and generously interpreting the facts that gave them their rise.

In one omission, however, Flash praises Bambaataa’s message of love and peace, but conspicuously fails to mention the many credible allegations of child sexual assault that marred Bambaataa’s later life and career. And Flash has gripes with how things went down. One of the most famous songs in the history of hip-hop, “The Message,” was released as a Grandmaster Flash and the Furious Five record, even though Flash and his Quik Mix Theory appear nowhere in its music. (“I think it would have been a bigger record had our formula as a group been on that record telling that story,” he wrote.) He doesn’t like that Herc claims to have invented the “merry-go-round” technique of multiple d.j.s taking turns on the table, balancing the beat together, without citing Flash. When everyone goes gaga for the practice of sampling, he feels left out in the cold: “It becomes weird and very alarming when you watch something—a concept, an idea, a practice, a love, a theory—that you created evolve in front of your eyes, and you do not get any credit for what that idea has been turned into.”

In 2007, Grandmaster Flash and the Furious Five became the first hip-hop act to enter the Rock & Roll Hall of Fame. In 2023, Flash was the subject of a soft-focus interview on the “Today” show, to celebrate the fiftieth anniversary of hip-hop’s invention. He emphasized his happiness at the genre’s development. “Something that is loved by so many people has to change and has to go through its changes and do different things,” he said. “It has to.”

Here’s all the credit he needs: get some friends together, ones who really know how to catch a beat and feel it in their bodies, put on a Grandmaster Flash record, and watch the world spin. ♦

title: Call of Duty introduces a gun skin that you can only see on an Xbox console
author: Morgan Park
content:
Call of Duty has joined Microsoft's bid to reinvigorate interest in Xbox consoles, today announcing a Modern Warfare 4 gun skin that you can only see if you're playing on an Xbox.

You read that right: The Inner Circuit blueprint is an M4 skin granted to those who pre-order Modern Warfare 4 on any platform, but the gun looks totally different on the Xbox version.

The Xbox 25th anniversary edition of the skin is designed after the green translucent plastic of the original Xbox console—it also features an Xbox logo and "Xbox 25" branding on the magazine. It looks, I must admit, pretty cool. Too bad these pictures are as close as I'll ever get to seeing it, as I don't own an Xbox.

Platform-specific incentives are nothing new for Call of Duty—for years, a Sony partnership meant PlayStation players got extra double XP, and Xbox used to get first dibs on map packs—but what's strange here is how this cosmetic isn't just exclusive to one platform, but only perceivable by it as well. If an Xbox player wants to show off their green M4 to a friend on PC, all they'll see is a boring-looking grey gun.

In a dedicated Xbox gun blog post, Activision clarified that in all ways other than appearance, the weapon blueprint is the same across platforms: "Both versions use the same attachments and perform identically in-game."

That's certainly one way to make pre-orders for a preferred platform more attractive, though this approach strikes me as more confusing than simply giving Xbox players a unique skin that everyone can see. At least that way I would actually know when the guy who killed me is trying to show off their fancy Xbox gun in a killcam. Instead, non-Xboxers who don't read Activision's blog or this website won't even know the difference. Strange!

And to think: This time last year, my PC was an Xbox.

title: "That is a lot of work": Persona 4 Revival producer says there's no plans for a Yosuke romance option, even if the team did think about it
author: Oisin Kuhnke
content:
Better luck next remake

While it's never been confirmed, some cut voice lines from the original release of Persona 4 indicated that once upon a time, the protagonist's right-hand party member Yosuke was romanceable. Instead what we ended up getting was a mostly quite homophobic character who never really moves past that mentality, though the upcoming Personal 4 Revival will apparently be changing Yosuke a bit. Though one thing it won't be doing, apparently, is adding that romance back in, even if the devs did consider it.

Speaking to GamesRadar about the requests for a romanceable Yosuke option in the remake, producer Kazuhisa Wada explained, "I was aware that some people were talking online about, like, 'Oh, Yosuke,' and they were kind of hoping for that. But we were thinking, if we did Yosuke, we kind of would have to do all the other male characters as well. And if we did that, that is a lot of work. So we were thinking about our time and schedule. I don't know if we could actually handle this, so we decided to let Yosuke float on by."

I'm certainly in two minds about this comment. On the one hand, it feels a touch like a cop out, as I don't even know why every main NPC has to be romanceable in the first place. On the other, I'm not sure I'd personally want a Yosuke romance. While Wada has admitted that Yosuke was "a little bit insensitive in terms of how he treats outsiders sometimes," and that the changes will make him fit better in "the world we live in now," I question what that means exactly.

Will he simply not be homophobic anymore? It's a quality quite baked into his character, and I'd rather a remake examine that and have his arc be more about confronting his bigoted opinions and apologising for the actions he took because of them. There is a general read on Yosuke that sees a lot of what he says as internalised homophobia too, but if the game were to just ignore he was ever like that and throw in a romance option, it would just feel like painting over a mouldy wall to me. Fingers crossed the changes feel natural at least.

title: Mortal Shell 2's latest update adds in an experimental new mode that adjusts the challenge based on how much you do or don't die
author: Oisin Kuhnke
content:
Prepare to try and not die

Another week, another Mortal Shell 2 update! The first proper one arrived a week ago, and smoothed down some of the game's rough edges to make for a (slightly) more generous experience. This next update brings with it a bevy of changes, but most notably is an experimental adaptive difficulty mode that changes depending how well you're doing.

It's all pretty simple. At times when you're doing well, taking down baddies and bosses without a hitch, they start to get harder. "Enemies gain damage, health and break resist, so they hit harder, take longer to bring down and are more difficult to stagger," a Steam blog post explains. "Keep clearing encounters without dying and enemies will scale well past the toughest the game was originally built to be, and they will keep climbing for as long as you keep winning."

On the opposite end of things, if you keep dying, your foes will weaken. They'll inversely do less damage, have less health and resist, "and a cap is applied so that no single attack can take more than a set fraction of your health bar, meaning you cannot be killed outright from full health." If you're playing in Night Mode, it should be noted, "these reductions do not apply." You should also be made aware that there is no visual indicator to show whether the game has gotten easier or harder, but there are plans to add something in further down the line.

The update goes a bit further than that too, with it now being possible to apply status effects to enemies when they're sorting themselves out after a riposte. In terms of balance, the update has "improved the logic around Gloom drops on death, making it easier for players to retrieve their lost Gloom." You'll also find a plethora of bug fixes, performance adjustments, audio tweaks, and even a few story changes.

title: Snapchat takes aim at Partiful with new event-planning features
author: Aisha Malik
content:
Snapchat announced on Thursday that it’s launching “Snapchat Plans,” a suite of features for creating, sharing, and managing real-world events with friends. The new event-planning features allow users to send and receive invitations and track details like the time, location, and attendees, all in one place.

Snapchat says the new features can be used to organize everything from birthday celebrations and sporting events to study sessions and weekend hangouts.

With Snapchat Plans, the social network is looking to take on Partiful, a popular event planning and digital invitation platform, as young users turn to dedicated apps to organize get-togethers rather than relying on group chats or social media. Snapchat isn’t the only tech company taking on Partiful and other invitation apps, as Apple launched an app called Invites last year that lets users create custom invitations for any occasion.

Snapchat users can create an event, called a “Snapchat Plan,” by adding a title, choosing a date and time, and inviting up to 200 friends. Invitations are then delivered directly within a one-on-one chat with each invited friend. Guests can then RSVP with “Going,” “Maybe,” or “Can’t Go.”

The app is also adding a new “My Plans” section on users’ profiles that lets them quickly browse all of their current, upcoming, and past Snapchat Plans. Additionally, once users click on a friend’s profile, they will see the events they share with them.

Once a Snapchat Plan is created, hosts can see who’s attending, invite more friends, and update event details as needed. Guests can view the full guest list, change their RSVP at any time, and get a reminder one hour before the event starts.

Although Snapchat has been a significant player in the social media space over the past decade, the company is now expanding its focus beyond how people communicate online to also help shape how they get together in the real world. This follows the broader trend that sees Gen Z looking for more in-person connections.

“No more missed get-togethers because of buried messages, lost details, or forgetting to create an invitation,” the company wrote in a blog post. “Snapchat Plans make it easier to organize these special in-person moments with your friends.”

Snapchat Plans are private and invite-only, the company says.

title: Claude, Codex, and Hermes installed unowned code inside corporate networks
content:
Documentation files on more than 100 websites are referencing potentially dangerous executable content that gets installed automatically when visited by many AI agents. A few dozen companies, some of them Fortune 500s, are among those that executed proof-of-concept code. At least one misconfigured site is directing visitors, human or AI, to live malware.

The potentially dangerous content is in llms.txt and llms-full.txt files, an emerging convention websites employ to provide machine-readable summaries of the site’s content and its high-level structure. These files are the AI equivalent of the robots.txt standard that instructs search engines how to index the site’s content. Google Lighthouse, a tool for helping web developers, has more here. Correctly configured llms.txt and llms-full.txt files for Cloudflare are here and here.

How the researchers found it

Researchers at a stealth startup in Israel scanned 6,214 live domains belonging to defense contractors, Fortune 500, and Big Tech companies. Of the 8,265 llms.txt and llms-full.txt files they found (many sites hosted both an llms.txt and an llms-full.txt file), 120 of them, each on a different site, pointed to one or more code packages or domain names that weren’t registered. To test what happens when an AI agent processes such files, the researchers registered a handful of the unclaimed names and hosted packages that caused any machine executing them to reach out to their server. Within an hour, the researchers received a phone-home response from a Fortune 500 company. Over time, they got a few dozen more, some from more Fortune 500 companies and others from startups. Their beacon also recorded the chain of parent processes that spawned each install, ultimately revealing that coding agents, including Claude, OpenAI’s Codex, and Nous Research’s Hermes, were involved. Anthropic, OpenAI, and Nous Research did not respond to requests for comment by the time of publication.

“The trust model is broken,” Alon Hertz, one of the researchers, wrote in an interview. “Agents treat vendor docs as ground truth and don’t question them—and neither do the humans supervising them. Agentic AI usage is exploding, and agents are spreading across every layer—SaaS, cloud, endpoint. As they multiply, so does the supply-chain surface, and today’s guards don’t cover it.”
